concepts.name: Khadi and Village Industries: Philosophy and Political Significance
key_dimensions: Distinction between Khadi as economic self-sufficiency vs. symbol of non-cooperation with British mills
Role of charkha (spinning wheel) as a unifying national symbol beyond mere economics
Gandhi vs. Nehru debate: Khadi as backward-looking romanticism vs. modernisation through industrialisation
Institutional legacy: All India Spinners Association (1925) and All India Village Industries Association (1934) — differences in scope and mandate

concepts.name: Village Sanitation as a Constructive Programme Item
key_dimensions: Gandhi's insistence that sanitation was more important than political independence — the 'sanitation before swaraj' argument
Link between untouchability abolition and manual scavenging/sanitation work
Contrast with colonial public health policies focused on urban centres
Relevance to Swachh Bharat Mission: Gandhian ideological roots vs. modern policy implementation

concepts.name: Nai Talim (Basic Education / Wardha Scheme, 1937): Structure and Ideology
key_dimensions: Core principle: craft-centred, self-financing education as opposed to colonial literary education
Zakir Husain Committee (1937) role in drafting the scheme — often confused with other committees
Criticism: opponents argued it would perpetuate caste-based vocational segregation (Ambedkar's critique)
Difference between Nai Talim and formal primary education under Congress provincial governments (1937–39)

concepts.name: Eradication of Untouchability (Harijan Welfare): Methods and Controversies
key_dimensions: Gandhi's use of 'Harijan' vs. Ambedkar's rejection of the term — ideological fault line
Harijan Sevak Sangh (1932): founding context (post-Poona Pact), structure, and limitations
Gandhi's method: moral persuasion of caste Hindus vs. Ambedkar's demand for political rights and reservations
UPSC trap: Poona Pact (1932) — what was conceded, what was withdrawn, and by whom

concepts.name: Communal Unity as a Constructive Programme Item: Strategy and Limitations
key_dimensions: Gandhi's approach: shared moral/spiritual values vs. political power-sharing formulas
Distinction between Gandhi's communal harmony efforts and Congress's formal constitutional negotiations with Muslim League
Role of constructive programme in Khilafat movement: communal unity through shared anti-imperialism
Why Gandhi considered communal unity a precondition for Swaraj — logical sequence in his 18-point programme

concepts.name: Women's Uplift in the Constructive Programme: Scope and Contradictions
key_dimensions: Gandhi's mobilisation of women in civil disobedience vs. his conservative views on women's primary domestic role
Specific items: removal of purdah, widow remarriage, opposing child marriage — what was included and excluded
Contrast with contemporary women's organisations (e.g., All India Women's Conference, 1927) on suffrage and legal rights
UPSC trap: Gandhi's constructive programme addressed women's 'uplift' but did NOT explicitly demand women's suffrage

concepts.name: Economic Equality and Trusteeship Theory: Gandhian Alternative to Socialism
key_dimensions: Trusteeship doctrine: wealthy as trustees of society's wealth — philosophical basis in Gita and Ruskin's 'Unto This Last'
Difference between trusteeship and socialist expropriation — Gandhi's explicit rejection of class struggle
Nehru/Congress Socialist Party critique: trusteeship as a utopian concept protecting capitalist interests
Post-independence relevance: 42nd Amendment (1976) inserted Gandhi's trusteeship principle into DPSP (Article 39) — fact check angle

concepts.name: Prohibition as a Constructive Programme Item: Social and Political Dimensions
key_dimensions: Gandhi's argument: alcohol as colonial revenue tool (excise) and instrument of social degradation of the poor
Link between prohibition and women's uplift — alcohol consumption linked to domestic violence and poverty
Congress provincial governments (1937–39): partial prohibition measures and their outcomes
UPSC trap: prohibition was in Gandhi's constructive programme AND is a DPSP (Article 47) — the ideological continuity

concepts.name: Hindi as Rashtrabhasha: Gandhi's Linguistic Nationalism and Its Limits
key_dimensions: Gandhi's promotion of Hindustani (Hindi-Urdu composite) vs. later demand for pure Hindi — distinction critical
Rashtrabhasha Prachar Samiti (Wardha, 1936): role and mandate
South Indian opposition: Periyar and Tamil leaders' resistance — early seeds of anti-Hindi agitation
UPSC trap: Gandhi supported 'Hindustani' not 'Hindi' — conflating the two is a common error

concepts.name: Kisan (Peasant) and Labour Welfare in the Constructive Programme
key_dimensions: Gandhi's approach: class collaboration (arbitration) vs. trade union/kisan sabha adversarial model
Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association (1918, TLA/Majoor Mahajan): Gandhi's model union — unique features
Distinction between Gandhi's constructive engagement with peasants and Congress Kisan Sabhas' radical demands
Why Gandhi opposed strikes as a first resort — philosophical basis and practical consequences

concepts.name: The Eighteen-Point Constructive Programme (1941 Pamphlet): Structure and Sequencing
key_dimensions: Original items vs. later additions — Khadi, village industries, village sanitation, new or basic education, adult education, uplift of women, education in health and hygiene, propagation of Rashtrabhasha, economic equality, kisans, labour, Adivasis, lepers, students
UPSC trap: the number of items changed across editions (1941 vs. 1945 expanded version) — candidates often misquote
Gandhi's argument that constructive programme was MORE important than civil disobedience for achieving Swaraj
Relationship between constructive programme and Lok Sevak Sangh: organisational vehicle Gandhi proposed

concepts.name: Tribal (Adivasi) Welfare in the Constructive Programme
key_dimensions: Gandhi's inclusion of Adivasi uplift as distinct from Harijan welfare — often conflated by candidates
Critique: Gandhi's approach seen as paternalistic and assimilationist vs. tribal autonomy demands
Contrast with Constituent Assembly debates on Fifth and Sixth Schedules — different approach to tribal rights
UPSC overlap: Thakkar Bapa's work among tribals — connected to both constructive programme and later tribal policy

concepts.name: Leprosy Work as a Constructive Programme Item: Social Significance
key_dimensions: Gandhi's personal engagement with leprosy patients as demonstration of anti-untouchability in practice
Leprosy work as bridge between sanitation, health, and social equality dimensions of constructive programme
Institutional legacy: Gandhi Memorial Leprosy Foundation — post-independence continuity
UPSC angle: least-discussed item in constructive programme — likely to appear as an odd-one-out or assertion-reason question

concepts.name: Constructive Programme vs. Civil Disobedience: Gandhi's Internal Debate
key_dimensions: Gandhi's 1940–41 position: constructive programme as the 'real' Swaraj preparation, mass civil disobedience as secondary
Difference between Individual Satyagraha (1940) and mass movement — why Gandhi chose individual over mass agitation
Quit India Movement (1942) context: Gandhi's frustration with slow constructive programme progress as trigger for mass action
UPSC trap: Gandhi did NOT abandon constructive programme during Quit India — the 'do or die' speech still referenced constructive work

concepts.name: Sarvodaya: Philosophical Foundation of the Constructive Programme
key_dimensions: Sarvodaya ('welfare of all') derived from Ruskin's 'Unto This Last' (1860) — Gandhi's translation and adaptation
Distinction: Sarvodaya vs. utilitarian 'greatest good of greatest number' — Gandhi's explicit rejection of majoritarianism
Post-Gandhi: Vinoba Bhave's Bhoodan/Gramdan movement as continuation of Sarvodaya — institutional evolution
UPSC trap: Sarvodaya is a philosophy underpinning constructive programme, NOT a specific programme item itself

concepts.name: All India Village Industries Association (AIVIA, 1934): Role and Distinction from AISA
key_dimensions: AIVIA focus: all village industries (oil pressing, tanning, soap-making) vs. All India Spinners Association (AISA, 1925) focused only on Khadi
J.C. Kumarappa's role as economist of AIVIA — his critique of industrial capitalism from Gandhian perspective
UPSC trap: candidates often merge AISA and AIVIA — year of founding, scope, and leadership differ
AIVIA's research and documentation of village industries as precursor to post-independence Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC)

concepts.name: Adult Education and Literacy in the Constructive Programme
key_dimensions: Distinction between Nai Talim (children) and adult literacy — separate items in the constructive programme
Gandhi's argument: political mobilisation requires literate, informed citizenry — functional link to Swaraj
Methods: night schools, reading circles attached to Congress committees at village level
Post-independence continuity: National Literacy Mission (1988) ideological lineage to Gandhian adult education

concepts.name: Constructive Programme and Panchayati Raj: Gandhi's Vision of Gram Swaraj
key_dimensions: Gram Swaraj as the ultimate goal: self-sufficient, self-governing village republic — 'oceanic circles' metaphor
Tension between Gandhi's village-centric vision and Ambedkar's view of villages as 'cesspools of capriciousness and ignorance'
UPSC trap: Panchayati Raj was NOT in the original 18-point constructive programme but was the institutional expression of Gram Swaraj
Constitutional reflection: Article 40 (DPSP) on Gram Panchayats and 73rd Amendment (1992) — ideological distance from Gandhi's vision

concepts.name: Student Participation in the Constructive Programme: Role and Boundaries
key_dimensions: Gandhi's specific advice to students: focus on constructive work over political agitation — often misread as discouraging student activism
Students as propagandists for Khadi, village sanitation, and literacy — specific assigned roles
Contrast: student role in Non-Cooperation (1920–22) — boycott of schools — vs. constructive programme emphasis on education
UPSC angle: Gandhi's evolving position on student participation in politics between 1920 and 1942
